title: Describing load: the home timeline
goal: By the end, you can describe a system's load with a few numbers, count what two ways of building a social feed cost, and explain why the biggest accounts decide the design.
opening:
Picture yourself opening a social app and pulling down to refresh. In under a second, you see the newest posts from the 200 accounts you follow. For almost everyone, that's easy work for the app.

Then a pop singer with 31 million followers posts a photo. For the next few minutes, posts arrive late for everybody, even the café's post about today's cake, which only 300 people follow.

The app's team had planned for the average account, and the average account has only about 200 followers. Averages are what every report shows first, and for most accounts they're the honest picture. They hide the one account that breaks the design.

The last lesson, Faults, failures and the people who run systems, ended with a promise: to measure how much work a system has to carry. In this lesson, we'll name the few numbers that decide that work, and count what two ways of building a feed cost. Then we'll handle the extremes that break each one. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A small social app has 100,000 users, and each follows 50 accounts, so the average account has about 50 followers. The app keeps a ready-made feed for every user: each new post is copied into the feed of each of its author's followers. Which number decides whether every post can reach all of its followers within 5 seconds?
options: The average number of followers, about 50
The total number of follows, about 5 million
The number of followers of the most-followed account
How many users are using the app at once
warmup.why: An average post needs 50 copies, which nobody notices. The deadline is broken by the account with the most followers. In this lesson's pretend network it has 67,725, so each of its posts needs 67,725 copies. If the app can make 5,000 copies a second, that's 13.5 seconds for one post. The average and the total describe the overall work well, and hide this case completely.

sections.h: Describing load: the few numbers that decide the cost
sections.body:
Let's leave the feed for a moment and take a simpler program: the one that records card payments for a café and the other shops it works for. Say it gets 2,000 requests a second. (A request is one message asking the program to do something.) That sounds like a description of its load, the amount of work coming in, but it can't tell you what will break first.

If those are 2,000 card payments, each a message of about 2 KB (about 2,000 characters), that's 4 MB a second of small, separate jobs. Each one needs a single quick trip to the database, the program that stores the payments. If they're 2,000 shop owners a second downloading a month of payments, 50 MB each, that's 100 GB a second. That needs different machines, a different way of storing data and a different design. Same rate, different systems.

So describing load means picking the few numbers that drive a system's cost. They're called its **load parameters**, and they come in a few kinds:

- rates: requests per second, posts per day, payments per hour at the busiest time of year;
- sizes: bytes per request, records touched per question;
- ratios: reads per write, which is how often data is looked at for each time it changes;
- counts per key, where a key is one account, one shop or one order: followers per account, payments per shop, items per order.

Report the peak, the busiest moment, as well as the average. In 2012, Twitter (the social network now called X) received about 5,000 posts a second on an average day, and over 12,000 during big events. Its record, in August 2013, was 143,199 posts in one second, during a Japanese TV showing of the film *Castle in the Sky*.

With the parameters in hand, you can ask the two questions that growing a system is about. If one parameter doubles and the machines stay the same, what happens to response time, how long each user waits for an answer? And if response time must stay the same, how many more machines do you need? When twice the machines carry twice the load at the same response time, the system has **linear scalability**. Usually the cost grows faster than that, and later lessons show why.

The last kind, counts per key, is the one people forget, because its average looks harmless. This lesson follows one system to show why: a social network's **home timeline**, the feed of recent posts by everyone a user follows. It's the best-documented load problem in public, because Twitter, X and Bluesky (a newer social network) have published their numbers. Its shape turns up in payments too, as the last section shows.

The lab builds a pretend network of 100,000 users who each follow 50 accounts. It picks them the way real networks grow, where a few accounts attract most of the follows. Here's how many followers each account ends up with:

```text
followers per account  mean 50.8   p50 21   p99 457   p99.9 2,733   max 67,725
```

Read it from the left. The mean is the ordinary average, 50.8. `p50` is the median: line the accounts up from fewest followers to most, and the one in the middle has 21. `p99` means 99 accounts in 100 have 457 followers or fewer, and `p99.9` means 999 in 1,000 have 2,733 or fewer. These are percentiles, the same measure the lesson Latency, percentiles and the tail used for waiting times.

The last number is the one that matters. The most popular account is followed by two thirds of all users, over 1,300 times the average. Every design in this lesson costs about the same for the median account. They differ on that last number.

**Describe a count per key as a spread, up to its maximum.**

Next, we'll try the simplest way to build a timeline, and count what it costs.

try.title: Describe the load of the pretend network
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the demo below. It builds the lab's pretend network (100,000 users, made from fixed random numbers with seed 42, so it's the same every time) and prints its load parameters first.
Before you look at the second line of numbers, predict the most accounts that one user follows. Ordinary users follow exactly 50.
Compare the two lines. Which one is skewed, with a few very large values, and where does the skew come from?

code.title: TimelineCostDemo.kt

try.expect:
The first block of output:

```text
load parameters of the network
  users                  100,000
  follow edges           5,079,000
  followers per account  mean 50.8   p50 21   p99 457   p99.9 2,733   max 67,725
  follows per account    mean 50.8   p50 50   p99 50   p99.9 50   max 4,000
```

A follow edge is one "this user follows that account" pair. The counts are exact on every machine, because the network comes from fixed random numbers. Both means are 50.8, since every follow has one follower and one account being followed. Followers are skewed, because each user picks popular accounts more often. Follows are flat except for the 20 heavy users the generator adds, who follow 4,000 accounts each. Those 20 are the second extreme this lesson deals with.

sections.h: Building each feed when it's read: fan-out on read
sections.body:
Start with the simplest design. Store each post once, next to its author, and build a timeline when someone asks for it. The mail room of a big office shows the idea. Say it keeps one pile of letters for each sender. When you come for your mail, a clerk goes through the piles of everyone you know and picks out what's new.

In a database, the piles are tables, which hold data in rows like a spreadsheet. A `posts` table holds one row per post, and a `follows` table holds one row for each "this user follows that account" pair. The query below asks for a timeline in SQL, the language most databases understand. You don't need to read SQL yet:

```sql
SELECT p.post_id, p.author_id, p.body
FROM follows f
JOIN posts p ON p.author_id = f.followee_id
WHERE f.follower_id = :me
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

In plain words: find every account that `:me` (the reader) follows, read the recent posts of each one, put them in order with the newest first, and keep 50. Posting is as cheap as it gets, one row. A read costs one lookup for every account followed, 50 in the lab's network. When one request causes many requests behind it, that's **fan-out**, and the number it causes is the fan-out factor. Here the fan-out happens when someone reads, so this design is called **fan-out on read**.

Now put in realistic load. The book *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, a well-known guide to building data systems, uses a model with round numbers. There are 500 million posts a day, about 5,800 a second, and users follow 200 accounts on average. And 10 million users are online, each refreshing their timeline every 5 seconds. That's 2 million timeline reads a second, each looking up about 200 piles: **400 million lookups a second**. And that's for the average user. A user who follows 4,000 accounts makes every one of their reads cost 4,000 lookups.

The cost isn't only work. A read that fans out to 200 lookups has to wait for the slowest of them. The lesson Latency, percentiles and the tail showed what that does: a lookup that is rarely slow turns into a read that is often slow. Say each lookup is slow 1% of the time. A read is fast only if all 200 lookups are fast, and 0.99 multiplied by itself 200 times (written 0.99^200) is about 0.13. So about 87% of reads hit at least one slow lookup.

Fan-out on read is still the right design when reads are rare or can't be predicted. Twitter's search worked this way. Each post was stored once, on one of many search computers, and a search asked every one of them and merged the answers. Nobody can prepare the answer to a search that nobody has typed yet. A home timeline is different. It's the same question, asked again and again, by every user, every few seconds.

**Prepare answers in advance only for questions that keep coming back.**

So why not prepare each timeline in advance? Next, we'll do exactly that.

try.title: Count the cost of fan-out on read
steps: Run the demo again (or scroll up to your last run) and find the `fan-out on read` row.
Predict before you look: the average and the largest number of lookups per read. Which user is behind the largest?
The `work per post` column adds one post's writes to the lookups of 60 reads, about Twitter's 2012 ratio of reads to posts. Note it down for the next section.
try.expect:
```text
                    writes per post     lookups per read   work per post     slowest
design                mean       max       mean      max   (60 reads)      delivery
fan-out on read        1.0         1       50.8    4,000          3,048          0.0 s
```

Every post costs exactly 1 write. The average read costs 50.8 lookups, one per account followed. The largest, 4,000, is one of the heavy users. `work per post` is 1 + 60 × 50.8 = 3,048. Delivery is instant, because a new post shows up on the next read with no extra work.

sections.h: Building each feed in advance: fan-out on write
sections.body:
Turn it around. Keep a ready-made timeline for every user: a list of post numbers, newest first. When Ana posts, the program looks up her followers and adds the new post's number to each follower's timeline. A read is now one lookup of one list that is already merged and in order. This design is called **fan-out on write**. In the mail room, it's a clerk who sorts every letter into each person's pigeonhole, their own small box on the wall, the moment it arrives. Collecting your mail takes a second.

The ready-made timeline is derived data, the idea from the lesson What a data system is. It's worked out from other data, so you could throw it away and rebuild it from the posts and the follows. A stored answer like this is called a materialized view. It exists only to make reads cheap, and you pay for it on every write. A post costs one write per follower of its author.

In the book's model, that's 5,800 posts a second × 200 followers, about **1.16 million timeline writes a second**. Fan-out on read needed 400 million lookups, so this is roughly 345 times less work. Why such a gap? Look at one author. Fan-out on write charges one write per follower each time the author posts. Fan-out on read charges one lookup per follower each time a follower reads. The follower count is the same on both sides. So for each author, the question is which happens more often, posting or reading. People read their timelines far more often than their friends post, so fan-out on write wins for nearly everyone.

It copes with bursts well, too. If 150,000 posts arrive in one second, the writes go into a queue, a list of jobs waiting to be done. Programs called fan-out workers take posts from the front of the queue and do the copying, and they catch up over the next few minutes. Posts appear a little late, and reads stay fast.

Twitter ran this design in 2012, as Raffi Krikorian, one of its engineers, described in a talk that year. Home timelines lived in Redis, a program that keeps data in the computer's memory, which is much faster to reach than a disk. Each timeline was capped at 800 entries and kept in 3 copies. Twitter served about 300,000 timeline reads a second, against about 5,000 new posts. The goal was to deliver each post to every follower within 5 seconds, and reaching 1 million followers took about 3.5 seconds.

Now take the singer from the opening. Lady Gaga had 31 million followers then, so one of her posts was **31 million writes**. At the rate that reached 1 million followers in 3.5 seconds, that's about 108 seconds, even with the fan-out workers to itself. The talk reported deliveries taking up to 5 minutes. The workers take posts from the queue in order, so the posts behind hers wait as well. A post from an account with 200 followers can't start until the 31 million writes ahead of it are done. That's the **celebrity problem**: one key with so many followers that its work holds up everyone else's.

**The cost of a post is its author's follower count. Find the largest one.**

The mail room has the same trouble: one sender mails 31 million people at once, and the clerks do nothing else all morning. Next, we'll handle that sender, and the reader at the other extreme.

try.title: Count the cost of fan-out on write
steps: Find the `fan-out on write` row in the demo's output.
Predict the slowest delivery. The demo's fan-out workers do 5,000 timeline writes a second, and you know the most-followed account from the first Try it.
Compare `work per post` with the fan-out on read row.
try.expect:
```text
design                mean       max       mean      max   (60 reads)      delivery
fan-out on write      50.8    67,725        1.0        1            111         13.5 s
```

Writes per post average 50.8, the average follower count, but one account's posts cost 67,725 writes. At 5,000 writes a second, that post takes 67,725 / 5,000 = 13.5 s to reach its last follower, even with an empty queue. Total work per post drops from 3,048 to 111 (50.8 + 60 × 1). So fan-out on write is 27 times cheaper overall, and still misses a 5-second target because of one account.

refs.title: Raffi Krikorian, Timelines at Scale (QCon San Francisco 2012)
High Scalability: The architecture Twitter uses to deal with 150M active users

sections.h: Handling the extremes: celebrities, heavy followers and the hybrid
sections.body:
The averages say fan-out on write. The extremes say it can't be the whole answer. There are two extremes, one on each side, and each gets its own fix.

The first is the celebrity. Don't fan out (copy into every follower's timeline) the posts of accounts with more than some number of followers. Store their posts once, in their own list, as fan-out on read does, and merge them into a follower's timeline when the follower reads. In the mail room, that sender's letters go on a table by the door, and each follower picks up a copy on the way out. A read then costs one lookup for the ready-made timeline, plus one for each celebrity the reader follows. Mixing the two designs like this is called a **hybrid**. Twitter's 2012 talk described this plan: stop fanning out the very largest accounts, and merge them in at read time.

Where should the line go? Work it out from the deadline. Say the fan-out workers do W writes a second, and a post must reach everyone within d seconds. Then no account with more than W × d followers can be fanned out in time. The demo's workers do 5,000 writes a second and the target is 5 seconds, so the threshold is 25,000 followers. Five accounts in the network are above it. Merging them makes the slowest delivery 4.7 s, and a read now costs 3.1 lookups on average instead of 1. Total work per post goes up, from 111 to 235. In this model, the hybrid does more work in total, and buys a deadline it can meet.

The model is a little unfair to the hybrid, because it charges for every follower's reads. In a real network, many of a celebrity's followers won't open the app before a post has dropped off the end of their 800 entries. The copies written for them are wasted work, which the hybrid avoids.

The second extreme is the **heavy follower**, who follows thousands of accounts and so receives a write for every post any of them makes. Bluesky described its fix in February 2025. Its timelines, for about 32 million users, lived in ScyllaDB, a database spread over many computers. Each user's timeline was kept together in one place, and one timeline write took about 600 µs (microseconds, millionths of a second). Users who followed hundreds of thousands of accounts overloaded the computers that held their timelines.

So Bluesky drops writes on purpose. A user receives a share of their timeline writes equal to `min(2000 / follows, 1)`: 2,000 divided by the number of accounts they follow, but never more than all of them. Follow 4,000 accounts, and half the writes are skipped. Follow 8,000, and three quarters are. Nobody reads 8,000 accounts' posts anyway, so they see a fair sample. Delivering a post from a large account used to take 5 to 10 minutes, and now took under 10 seconds. Even the slow cases improved: the time that 99 posts in 100 beat, from first write to last, fell by over 96%.

Here the mail room picture breaks. No mail room throws away three quarters of someone's letters, but a skipped post costs its reader almost nothing.

The product can change the load as well. In 2023, X published the code behind its For You timeline, which is no longer "everyone I follow, newest first". Each request gathers about 1,500 candidate posts, roughly half from followed accounts and half from others. A machine-learning model, a program trained on past clicks and likes to guess what you'll enjoy, ranks them. A program called Home Mixer then puts the timeline together. Much of that work happens when the user reads, because the ranking depends on the user and the moment.

So here is the method. Name the load parameters. Find the extreme that dominates the cost. Prepare answers in advance where reads dominate. Handle each extreme on its own, and accept a little imperfection where users can't see it.

**Size a design for its largest key, not its average one.**

This lesson counted work and left out machines. All of it still has to run somewhere, and one computer only goes so far.

aside.title: Does this happen with payments too?
aside.body: Yes, with shops in place of celebrities. Say the payments app keeps a running balance for each shop, and every payment updates it: a ready-made answer, like a ready-made timeline. That's right for almost every shop. Then a concert ticket shop opens its sales and takes 3,000 payments a second, and every one of them waits its turn to update the same balance. The fix is the one from this section: treat the extreme key on its own, for example by splitting its balance into several parts that a read adds up. And describe the load per key (payments per shop at the median, the p99 and the maximum) as well as payments per second.

try.title: Move the threshold and the read ratio
steps: Run the demo with a threshold of 2,000 followers by adding `-Pargs='2000 60'` to the command. Predict first: what happens to the slowest delivery, and to lookups per read?
Run it with `-Pargs='25000 0.5'`: the same hybrid, but users read only half as often as they post. Which design is cheapest now, and why?
Find the hybrid's average writes per post with a threshold of 1,000,000 (`-Pargs='1000000 60'`), where nobody counts as a celebrity. It's below fan-out on write's 50.8. What removed those writes?
try.expect:
Threshold 2,000:

```text
hybrid > 2,000        41.0     1,978       10.4      157            663          0.4 s
celebrities (more than 2,000 followers): 157 accounts
```

Delivery drops to 0.4 s, but 157 accounts are now merged at read time, so a read costs 10.4 lookups on average and up to 157. A lower threshold buys faster delivery with more expensive reads.

At 0.5 reads per post, `work per post` is 26 for fan-out on read, against 51 for fan-out on write and 50 for the hybrid. When users read less often than they post, fan-out on read is cheaper. At a threshold of 1,000,000, the hybrid's average is 50.4 writes, not 50.8. The 20 heavy users follow 4,000 accounts each, so Bluesky's rule keeps only half of their writes.

twitter/the-algorithm: the code behind X's For You timeline

compare.title: The same timeline, built at read time and at write time

a.label: fan-out on read
a.title: on every read: one lookup per account followed
a.src:
-- a post is one INSERT into posts
-- a read builds the timeline:
SELECT p.post_id, p.author_id, p.body
FROM follows f
JOIN posts p ON p.author_id = f.followee_id
WHERE f.follower_id = :me
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

b.label: fan-out on write
b.title: Redis lists, the way Twitter kept timelines in 2012
b.src:
# on every post by author A: one write per follower
for f in followers(A):
    LPUSH timeline:f <post id>     # newest at the front
    LTRIM timeline:f 0 799         # keep 800 entries

# on every read: one lookup
LRANGE timeline:me 0 49

compare.note: Both return the 50 newest posts by the accounts `:me` follows. The query on the left does its work every time someone reads, and its cost grows with how many accounts the reader follows. The loop on the right does its work once per post, and its cost grows with how many followers the author has. It uses three Redis commands: `LPUSH` adds a post number to the front of a list, `LTRIM` cuts the list to its first 800 entries, and `LRANGE` reads entries 0 to 49. `LTRIM` is why a ready-made timeline stays a fixed size: old entries fall off the end, and a user who scrolls past them falls back to a slower path.

worked.title: Count both designs' costs at the book's numbers, and pick a threshold

steps.say: Write down the load parameters. The book's model has 500 million posts a day, 200 follows (and so 200 followers) per user on average, and 10 million users online, each refreshing every 5 seconds. A day has 86,400 seconds.
Fan-out on read pays on every read: one lookup per account followed.
Fan-out on write pays on every post: one write per follower. Each read becomes one lookup.

Check the extremes. Suppose the fan-out workers are sized for the average, about 1.2 million writes a second, and a post must reach everyone in 5 seconds. One post from an account with 100 million followers then needs almost a minute and a half, and every post behind it waits.

Set the celebrity threshold from the deadline: the lab's `celebrityThreshold` is writes per second times the deadline (`floor` rounds down to a whole number). Accounts above 6 million followers are merged at read time, and everyone else is fanned out.
steps.code:
fun celebrityThreshold(writesPerSecond: Double, deadlineSeconds: Double): Long =
    floor(writesPerSecond * deadlineSeconds).toLong()

celebrityThreshold(1_200_000.0, 5.0)   // 6,000,000 followers

lab.title: Build fan-out on write and the hybrid
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. All 9 fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a `TODO`. Nothing else needs to be installed or started: everything is counted, not timed.
Read `Timelines.kt`. `Work` counts writes and lookups, and `FanOutOnRead` is the finished design to compare against. The tests check your timelines against it, so read how it merges lists.
In `Designs.kt`, write `FanOutOnWrite`: one `ArrayDeque` (a list you can add to at either end) per user, newest first, cut to `cap` entries. Count one write per follower and one lookup per read.

Write `lossFactor` (Bluesky's `min(2000 / follows, 1)`), then `Hybrid`. Celebrities are stored once. Everyone else is fanned out, except the writes that `sample(postId, follower)` says to drop for heavy followers. A read is one lookup, plus one per celebrity followed.

In `Delivery.kt`, write `deliverySeconds` (one first-in, first-out queue on a pretend clock) and `celebrityThreshold`. Run the tests until all 9 pass. One uses jqwik, a library that checks a rule against many random inputs: it checks that all three designs give every user the same timeline.
hints: Post numbers grow with time, so `addFirst` keeps a timeline sorted newest first. `take(limit)` on an `ArrayDeque` gives you the read.
Work out in the `Hybrid` constructor which followed accounts of each user are celebrities. Then a read doesn't have to scan all of a user's follows to find the few lists to merge.

In the hybrid, merge `timeline.take(limit)` with `recent(celebrityPosts, limit)` for each celebrity, then `sortedDescending().take(limit)`. Taking more than `limit` from each list never changes the answer.
For `deliverySeconds`, keep one variable: the time at which the queue is next free. A post starts at `max(arrival, queueFreeAt)`.
If the property test fails, it prints the seed and the user. A celebrity threshold of 0, which makes every author with a follower a celebrity, is a good edge case to think through.

drill.title: The hybrid's read, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `homeTimeline` for the hybrid. You have the user's ready-made timeline (newest first, in `timelines[user]`), the celebrities they follow (`celebritiesFollowed[user]`), and each celebrity's posts, oldest first, in `celebrityPosts`. Count the lookups and return the newest `limit` post numbers.

recap: Load, the work coming in, is described by a few load parameters: rates, sizes, ratios and counts per key. Report the peak and the whole spread, not only the average.
Fan-out on read stores a post once and does the work on every read: one lookup per account followed. It suits rare or unpredictable reads, like search.
Fan-out on write keeps a ready-made timeline per user, a materialized view, and pays one write per follower. For each author, it wins whenever followers read more often than the author posts.
The extremes break each design: a celebrity's post is millions of writes that delay every post behind it, and a heavy follower makes reads, or writes, expensive.
Hybrids handle the extremes separately: merge accounts above W × deadline followers at read time, and drop some writes for heavy followers, as Bluesky's `min(2000 / follows, 1)` does.
The limit: this lesson counted work, not machines. It doesn't say how many computers the work needs, or what to do when one computer is no longer enough.
closing:
We started with a pop singer whose one post made everyone's feed late, in a network where the average account looked harmless. The cost of a post is its author's follower count, and one huge count decided the design. The fix was to treat that account, and the heavy followers, on their own.

Open an app you use that shows counts, such as followers, likes or reviews. Find the largest count you can, and compare it with a typical one. That ratio is the number its designers had to plan for.

Next, we'll ask what to do when one computer can't carry the load: buy a bigger one, or add more.

quiz.q: An account posts 20 times a day. Each of its 10,000 followers opens the app 3 times a day. Counting only this account's posts, which design does less work?
options: Fan-out on write: 10,000 writes is less than 30,000 lookups
Fan-out on read: 30,000 lookups a day against 200,000 writes
They are equal, because both are proportional to 10,000 followers
Fan-out on write, because reads are always more expensive than writes
quiz.why: Fan-out on write pays 10,000 writes for each of 20 posts: 200,000 a day. Fan-out on read pays one lookup of this account's list each time a follower reads: 10,000 × 3 = 30,000. The follower count appears on both sides and cancels, so what decides is posts per day against reads per day per follower. This author posts more often than the followers read. The first option counts only one post.

quiz.q: With fan-out on read, a timeline read looks up the lists of 200 followed accounts at once and waits for all of them. Each lookup is slow 1% of the time, independently of the others. About what share of reads are slow?
options: About 87%
Every read
quiz.why: A read is fast only if all 200 lookups are fast: 0.99^200 ≈ 0.13. So about 87% of reads wait for at least one slow lookup. This is the fan-out effect from Latency, percentiles and the tail: a rare slow case for each lookup becomes the normal case for each read. 1% would be right for a read that makes one lookup, and "every read" ignores the 13% of reads that still get lucky.

quiz.q: Your fan-out workers do 400,000 timeline writes a second in total, and a post must reach every follower within 5 seconds. Above what follower count should the hybrid stop fanning out an account?
options: 2,000,000 followers
80,000 followers
400,000 followers
Any account above the average follower count
quiz.why: The threshold is writes per second times the deadline: 400,000 × 5 = 2,000,000 writes, the most one post can need and still finish in time with the workers to itself. 80,000 divides instead of multiplying. Merging everyone above the average would turn most reads into expensive merges, and throw away the reason for preparing timelines in advance.

quiz.q: Bluesky's rule gives each user `min(2000 / follows, 1)` of their timeline writes. A user follows 10,000 accounts. What happens to the posts of the accounts they follow?
options: All of them arrive, just later
About 20% of them are written into this user's timeline and the rest are skipped
About 80% of them are written and 20% are skipped
Only the posts of the 2,000 most popular accounts arrive
quiz.why: 2,000 / 10,000 = 0.2, so each post lands in this user's timeline with a chance of 0.2, and the other 80% of the writes never happen. The sample is spread over all 10,000 accounts, not cut off at the most popular 2,000. Nothing is delayed: the writes are dropped on purpose, because nobody reads 10,000 accounts' posts.

quiz.q: One first-in, first-out fan-out queue does 100,000 writes a second. A celebrity post needing 3,000,000 writes enters at t = 0 s. A post with 300 followers enters at t = 1 s. How long after it arrives does the small post reach all its followers?
options: 3 ms
About 30 s
About 29 s
1 s
quiz.why: The celebrity post holds the queue until 3,000,000 / 100,000 = 30 s. The small post arrives at 1 s, starts at 30 s and needs 300 / 100,000 = 3 ms, so it finishes at 30.003 s, about 29 s after it arrived. 3 ms is its own fan-out time with an empty queue, and 30 s measures from t = 0 instead of from its arrival. This wait behind the job at the front of the queue is why one celebrity hurts everyone's delivery.

flashcards.back: A post is 1 write, to the author's own list. A read is one lookup per account the reader follows, plus a merge.

flashcards.back: From the deadline: fan-out writes per second × seconds allowed. Accounts with more followers than that can't be fanned out in time, so merge them in at read time.

terms.plain: A number that describes how much work a system gets and drives its cost, such as requests per second or followers per account.
Twice the machines carry twice the load at the same response time.
One request causing many requests behind it; the fan-out factor is how many.
Store each item once, and put the answer together when someone reads it.
Copy each new item into every place that will read it, so a read is one lookup.
The feed of recent posts by everyone a user follows.
One key with so many followers, or so much traffic, that work that grows with it breaks the design.
Skipping some fan-out writes on purpose for heavy followers, users who follow so many accounts that they could never read every post.

explain_back.prompt: A friend asks why a social network that prepares every user's timeline in advance would still merge some posts in when the user reads. Explain it with numbers.
explain_back.answer: Preparing in advance means every post is copied into each follower's timeline, so a post costs one write per follower and a read costs one lookup. For the average account that's a great deal, because people read far more often than their friends post. But the cost of a post is its author's follower count, and some counts are enormous. An account with 31 million followers needs 31 million writes per post. If the fan-out workers do about 285,000 writes a second, that's well over a minute and a half per post, and every ordinary post queued behind it waits too. So accounts above a threshold, the workers' writes per second times the delivery deadline, are stored once and merged into a follower's timeline at read time. That makes reads a bit more expensive, one extra lookup per celebrity followed, and keeps delivery within the deadline for everyone else.

deeper.body:
**Weighted costs.** This lesson counted a write and a lookup as one unit each. They aren't equal in practice. Twitter sent timeline writes in batches of thousands, while a fan-out-on-read lookup is a separate read that the reader waits for. Give them weights, `c_w` per write and `c_l` per lookup, and the rule for each author becomes: fan out on write when `posts × c_w < reads × c_l`. The follower count still cancels. What doesn't cancel is *who waits*. Fan-out on read puts the cost on the reader's response time. Fan-out on write puts it on delivery time, which a queue can absorb.

**How Bluesky stored its timelines.** The timelines were split into hundreds of shards, slices of the data held by different computers, and each user's timeline sat whole in one of them. Writing a post to 1,000 timelines at once took about 1.2 s, and the slowest 1% of single writes took up to 15 ms. Copying one post to 2,000,000 followers, one write at a time, would have taken about 20 minutes (2,000,000 × 600 µs).

**Caching the extremes.** Bluesky's rule needs each user's follow count on every fan-out. Its post says the counts for users who follow many accounts are kept in Redis as a sorted list, reloaded every 30 seconds. Without that saved copy, the lookups would add over a million reads a second to the main database. Even the fix for one extreme had to be designed around another load parameter.

**Why the lab drops writes by a fixed rule.** `sample(postId, follower)` turns the pair into a fixed number between 0 and 1 (a hash: the same input always gives the same number). So the same post is kept or dropped for the same follower every time you run the code, and the tests can be exact. A real system could use a random number. A fixed one also means that a fan-out job that runs again drops the same writes, instead of filling in some it skipped the first time.

**The opposite pattern, on purpose.** Twitter's search index, Earlybird, was built on Lucene, a free library for search indexes, and held in memory. It stored each post on one machine and asked every machine at query time: fan-out on read, because nobody can prepare the answer to a search that hasn't been typed. Most large systems use both patterns, chosen for each feature from that feature's load parameters.
